summary:
This is a 1997 National Park Service oral history with Minnie Rodwin (née Mary Floun), recorded at her daughter's home in Sunrise, Florida when she was ninety. Born Christmas morning 1907 in London's East End to Polish-Jewish parents who ran a bakery on Commercial Road, she crossed on the Philadelphia in September 1910 at age three. Her father Morris had left the year before, called back into the Russian army — conscription, not persecution, was the precipitating motive. The family followed once he had purchased tickets and had kin waiting in New York.

Four threads carry the material. The departure-costs thread follows the staged exit: army recall, purchased tickets, a year alone in New York, the steerage crossing at the bottom of the ship, and a mother who forbade tip-taking. The livelihoods thread is almost entirely about baking — mother Sophie carried the trade from Warsaw through London to 141 Essex Street, where the bakery became Floun's and lasted about fifteen years before moving it to Rockaway Beach; father Morris, originally a tailor, learned the trade from his wife. School authorities directed the older brothers to stay home and help; children topped macaroons at the holidays. The regional-networks thread shows Polish-Jewish kin across New York (Forty-Second Street, the Bronx, 'all over') gathering every Friday at the father's bakery, with Rodwin's home later serving as the standing meeting place. The toll thread holds two separations — daughters left with grandmother until one was seven — and the family's resettlement into a four-story walkup tenement with shared bathrooms and coin-operated gas meters.

What is thin: the bureaucratic and economic texture of departure — no Ellis Island memory, no fare specifics beyond 'tickets.' What is unresolved: whether the planned reunion with the sisters ever happened. What is missing: any sense of how the bakery fared economically beyond its name and fifteen-year run.

brief: Minnie Rodwin's 1997 oral history is short (27 minutes) and warm, but memory at ninety is patchy: she cannot recall Ellis Island, the bakery's formal name, or whether the Polish sisters ever rejoined the family. Father Morris's conscription-driven departure anchors the narrative. The material rewards cluster around baking — mother's trade, carried from Warsaw through London to 141 Essex Street and on to Rockaway Beach — and around the kin network that gathered weekly at the bakery. The Lower East Side tenement is described only in address and walkup height. Look for material addressing the reunion with the sisters, Ellis Island processing, or the bakery's economic survival.
